books.section: Topic 4.6 Market Revolution: Society and Culture, C. Workers and New Methods of Production
The North and the Textile Industry

stimulus.text: A magazine cover from August 1845. The title “LOWELL OFFERING” arches over a scene of a young woman in a long dress holding a book, with mill buildings behind her and a beehive at the left. Below the scene, the cover reads: “A REPOSITORY OF ORIGINAL ARTICLES, WRITTEN BY “FACTORY GIRLS.”” The publisher’s line reads “LOWELL: MISS CURTIS & FARLEY. 1845.”
stimulus.source_note: Cover of the Lowell Offering, August 1845, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain). Image viewed before writing; cover text transcribed from the image.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The women who wrote the Lowell Offering were

options.text: the wives of the mill owners who ran the boardinghouses
options.misconception: The cover says the articles were written by factory girls, not by the owners' wives.

options.text: young women working in the Lowell textile mills
women reformers in Boston who had never worked in a mill
options.misconception: The writers were the mill workers themselves, not outside reformers in Boston.

options.text: the daughters of Southern planters visiting New England
options.misconception: The writers were Northern mill workers, not visitors from Southern plantations.

rationales.A: The cover names the writers as factory girls, the young women working in the mills. The owners' wives ran boardinghouses; they did not write the magazine.
rationales.B: The cover calls the magazine a repository of original articles written by factory girls. Those writers were the young women tending the looms in Lowell's textile mills.
rationales.C: The cover says the articles were written by factory girls. The writers worked in the mills; they were not Boston reformers writing about mills from outside.
rationales.D: The writers were Lowell mill workers from New England farm families. Southern planters' daughters had no part in this magazine.
rationales.general:
1. Read the cover line under the picture. It names the writers plainly.
2. Ask who a factory girl was. She was a young woman working in a Lowell textile mill.
3. Match the words to the workers. The magazine was written by the mill hands themselves.
Background: The Lowell mills hired farm daughters for a few years, housed them in company boardinghouses, and paid them cash wages.
Remember: a cover tells you who made a source, so read its title lines before you read anything else.
